fields.title: Level 0 Peasants
fields.text: In this introductory adventure, every player controls multiple level 0 peasants. They have no special abilities and die in a single hit; the multiple peasants give players "extra lives" while they learn the system.

fields.title: The GLOG Is Modular
fields.text: Treat the GLOG as a philosophy rather than a single unified ruleset: take the rules you like, discard the rules you do not, and assemble the game suited to your group from many sources.

fields.title: DM Authority over the Rulebook
fields.text: The rulebook is never a higher authority than the DM. The "True GLOG" is the version the group builds for itself.

fields.title: No Initial Light Sources or Necessary Tools
fields.text: Level 0 peasants are not initially provided with light sources or necessary tools, allowing mechanics, including the darkness rules, to be introduced one at a time.

fields.title: Plan, Avoid, or Flee Battles
fields.text: Players should spend more time choosing and planning battles than fighting them. Running away is often the right choice, and the most reliable ways to kill a monster do not rely on attack rolls.

fields.title: Social Play without Social Stats
fields.text: There are no social stats or abilities. To be effective, players must learn what creatures want, usually by asking them.

fields.title: Optional Secrets Improve Survival
fields.text: The adventure contains over a dozen secret doors and hidden treasures, ranging from obvious to cryptic. None are essential, but all improve the party's odds of survival.

fields.title: Information Is a Resource
fields.text: Information is used to find secrets, solve puzzles, and sidestep combats. Players acquire more information by asking questions about the environment and should try to ask a question in every room.

fields.title: Solve Puzzles with Patterns and Mundane Objects
fields.text: Many puzzles are solved by recognizing patterns or using mundane objects cleverly. Many have three or more solutions, and many problems can be solved with enough rope.

fields.title: Use the Dungeon's Interconnections
fields.text: The dungeon's rooms are tightly interlinked through backtracking, loops, and mapping. A solution to a puzzle or combat may be found in a later room, and an encounter need not be handled in the room where it occurs.

fields.title: Balance Time Pressure against Investigation
fields.text: Time is the enemy: torches burn down, the party has no food or water, and every 30 minutes carries a risk of a Random Encounter. Survival also requires taking time to investigate suspicious phenomena, so players must balance these competing needs.

fields.title: Treat the Whole Dungeon as the Obstacle
fields.text: Do not treat the dungeon as isolated rooms that each contain an encounter that must be resolved before continuing. The obstacle is the entire dungeon simultaneously, not only the current room.

fields.title: Give More Information When in Doubt
fields.text: When in doubt, give the players more information rather than less.

fields.title: Frame Multiple Viable Options
fields.text: Engagement increases when players receive meaningful decisions. Frame situations so the players have multiple viable options.

fields.title: Telegraph Danger and Provide Options
fields.text: Horrible threats must leave players either an option to choose another path or options to recover. Presenting a sagging floor and asking whether they enter is an option; an unannounced lethal hazard resolved only by a Dexterity check is mere chance and offers no meaningful choice.

fields.title: Let Choices and Luck Matter
fields.text: If a player makes a mistake or gets unlucky, allow the character to die rather than rescuing them and cheapening their choices. Conversely, allow lucky outcomes and good schemes that appear to "cheat" the game.

fields.title: Allow Combat to Be Skipped or Trivialized
fields.text: If players find a way to skip or trivialize a combat, allow it. Combats are obstacles that may be manipulated as well as brute-forced, not mandatory encounters that must be consumed routinely.

fields.title: Do Not Impose Morality
fields.text: Do not impose the DM's morality on the players. Their actions have consequences, but conscientious or humanistic behavior must remain a player-driven choice, even if they choose to be murderhobos.

fields.title: Keep Time Measures
fields.text: Track time. Actions such as digging through bone piles may cost only time; searching for useful items therefore spends torchlight and accepts the risk of random encounters.

fields.title: Never Fudge or Retune Mid-Encounter
fields.text: Never fudge the dice or alter a creature or trap during an encounter. If combat is too difficult, the PCs can flee using Pursuit; if it is too easy, wrap it up quickly and move on using Morale.

fields.title: Do Not Hint at Missed Secret Areas
fields.text: Players will not find every secret area; resist the temptation to drop hints.

fields.title: Reward Attentive and Investigative Play
fields.text: Good play is not defined by strong character builds or thorough rules knowledge. It comes from being attentive, investigative, meticulous, scheming, and cowardly, except when a situation demands suicidal boldness.

fields.title: Do Not Reveal Missed Content after the Session
fields.text: After the session, never tell players about what they missed. The dungeon's secrets must be earned through play or remain undiscovered.
